We investigate the time evolution of a second class particle in an ASEP model with periodic boundaries and uniform particle flow velocities. We represent the system's state using a DPH (Alternating Asymmetric Particle Exchange) configuration and demonstrate that, at any given point in time, the distribution of particles can be divided into three distinct, independent ASEP segments. By leveraging the established SSD (Stochastic Vertex Model) integrability of the ASEP model, we establish an integrality relation for the time-dependent ASEP dynamics and derive a novel integrality connection for the second class particle's dynamics within the ASEP framework.

Finding an exact solution to differential models and matching them with actual data are key steps in applying mathematical models, specifically ordinary differential equations models, to real-world problems.  It is crucial to ensure that the obtained solutions are not only precise but also biologically feasible, particularly when dealing with quantities that must be non-negative.  While methods for assessing the biological plausibility of ODE models have been established, a systematic approach for ensuring solutions align with data biologically has not been previously developed.  This study introduces such a method, along with a numerical example to illustrate its application.  It is shown that the data obtained from a biologically infeasible model can be reconciled through a transformation of the differential equations, providing a pathway to obtain accurate and feasible models from initial estimates.

We employ an effective non-rigid pendulum model to uncover the underlying
mechanics of both coherent atom-molecule conversion and subsequent instability
onset. Utilizing this model, we derive an effective potential and identify the
conditions for the existence of a pendulum, which in turn dictate the point of
backreaction-induced instability onset. Furthermore, we uncover a connection
between the minimal oscillation energy of the effective pendulum and the coherent
field evolution, which in turn provides an efficient method for determining the
coherence lifetime.

DNA data storage is an emerging technology that leverages massive storage capacities, but it faces significant challenges in efficiently managing vast storage partitions. In this research, we present a novel, practical design for primers that enhances the efficiency of random access and sorting processes within a DNA storage system. Our primers' design incorporates a strategic element - a set of subsets with distinct sets of storage partitions, enabling a group of subsets to correspond to multiple sets with different management strategies. This design allows for scalable access and sorting by a set of subsets, and provides flexible management of storage partitions. Moreover, our design offers adjustable complexity for the random access and sorting processes, and can accommodate a wide range of data packing rates. It also comes with a set of performance guarantees, including a set of theorems that describe the minimum/maximum number of subsets and primers, and a set of lemmas that outline the steps to create a set of subsets with a particular property. Overall, our design for primers offers a robust, flexible solution for efficiently managing storage partitions in DNA data storage systems.

This study introduces a novel method, PCGA, for spatial and temporal interpolation of riverbed bathymetry using acoustic Doppler current profiler (ADCP) measurements. The effectiveness of PCGA is evaluated in comparison to traditional techniques like kriging and the principal component geostatistical approach developed by Xu et al. (2019). The study involves analyzing time-varying flow velocities within a meandering reach of the Yangtze River, with results showing that PCGA can accurately capture spatial flow patterns and local bedforms, and provides reliable flow velocity estimates in flow cross-sections where measurements are sparse. The study also identifies the importance of considering flow velocity variability along the riverbed and recommends incorporating spatial covariance of the principal component scores in the PCGA estimation model.

In this paper, a method is proposed to evaluate the effectiveness of automatic exposure settings in selecting high dynamic range (HDR) image sets. A dynamic weight-based metric is used to combine multiple indicators, including the average and range of HDR values, to determine the optimal exposure settings for a given scene. The algorithm begins by randomly selecting initial camera parameters and iteratively adjusts them based on exposure quality in order to produce a highly consistent HDR image set. The method, which is based on a stochastic optimization approach, requires only the ability to preview single images and does not directly interact with the camera hardware. Furthermore, the algorithm can be applied to both digital stills and video footage.

The rapid development of causal deep learning has been hindered by a lack of structured organization, making it difficult to pinpoint research gaps and assess the consistency of evaluation methods. To address this issue, we present CausalCLex, a comprehensive framework that systematically groups 20 21-state-of-the-art methods across four fundamental causal learning challenges using standard deep learning evaluations. By examining a diverse array of benchmarks, our analysis reveals the underlying consistency of current evaluation practices. As a result, CausalCLex serves as a consistent reference point that researchers can use to explore causal learning through typical deep learning assessments, identify research gaps, and assess the methodological consistency of training and evaluation procedures.

The renowned Madsen-Weiss theorem, which establishes a b-principle and a form of K-theoretic stability for the oriented closed block cobordism theory of high-dimensional 2-blocks, can be seen as a topological variant of the classical Borel conjecture for certain families of surface groups, specifically in a range related to the point where a corresponding L-theoretic stability phenomenon ends.

This research provides a detailed analysis of the Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) method when used with a specific coarse space based on local problem solutions. The BDDC algorithm is an effective strategy for solving problems using non-conforming finite elements, particularly when dealing with complex, irregular computational grids. The performance of the BDDC method with this specific preconditioner is demonstrated to be bounded, with an exponential increase limited to the square of a specific parameter (theta), related to the relationship between element sizes in different subdomains. The proof of this performance involves utilizing a continuous extension operator, with BDDC methods of first type being directly applicable when the finite element mesh is shape regular and of second type when the mesh is irregular. Furthermore, the analysis shows that the BDDC method achieves optimal scalability on problems with varying mesh sizes, while maintaining efficiency for eigenvalue problems with solutions that have local regularity properties.

The standard approach to diffusion analysis relies on separating time-series data into independent realizations, a method that fails to account for the influence of correlations and heterogeneity, key features present in climate systems. The underlying assumption of Gaussian diffusion can be significantly altered by these elements, potentially leading to the emergence of non-identical diffusion timescales and the absence of central limit theorem conditions, which would result in the absence of symmetric probability distributions. The primary objective of this study is to develop a statistical framework that incorporates correlations and heterogeneity, and to apply this framework to investigate their effects on the diffusion timescale and symmetry of the resulting probability distributions. The methodology involves applying our diffusion test to both synthetic models and real-world temperature anomalies from the HadCRUT4 dataset, and the findings reveal that models and regions with heterogeneous properties exhibit altered diffusion timescales and asymmetric probability distributions.

We investigate the interaction between multiple counterpropagating optical modes in an optical loop resonator and derive a set of coupled-power equations that describe this interaction. These equations show that the cross-phase modulation effect is significantly more pronounced than self-phase modulation in identical modes, leading to a more efficient nonlinearity for all-signal-based modulation. By solving the coupled-power equations, we analyze the backscattered power in an empty resonator and one containing a single bright soliton. Notably, in the presence of the soliton, the backscattered power exhibits a large DC offset and an oscillating component with a much greater amplitude than that in the empty case, thus demonstrating direct and highly sensitive all-optical mass sensing in the time domain with unprecedented sensitivity.

A new, innovative model known as a multiscale enhanced super-resolution GAN has been developed to capture the complex patterns of turbulent flow in a channel. This research compares our proposed 100-times smaller scale model to an equivalent four-times larger scale model, revealing that the smaller model outperforms its larger counterpart. Furthermore, it has been discovered that the performance of these models varies significantly based on the Reynolds number. Specifically, the performance drop for the Nx8 model is more pronounced at a lower Reynolds number of 3000 compared to a higher one of 5000.

In order to assess how reinforcement learning algorithms perform in complex and dynamic environments, it is crucial to conduct experiments in settings that are carefully managed and well-defined. However, most papers that propose new algorithms often perform them in completely different environments, making it difficult to evaluate their performance under consistent conditions. To address this issue, we present a unified framework consisting of five distinct, dynamic traffic scenarios that progress through a series of staged changes in their design. By implementing incremental and controlled modifications in these scenarios, researchers can evaluate the performance of algorithms as they adapt to evolving conditions. We apply this framework to the Successive Regularized Greedy Policy algorithm, allowing us to examine its behavior in response to environmental changes across a wide range of parameters.

We present an evolution analysis method for dynamic process models based on DCR graphs, allowing us to investigate how processes change over time. Our approach involves creating a "dynamic vocabulary" to capture the concepts used in observations, and then representing the evolution of processes using compact "snapshots" at various time points. By analyzing the differences between these snapshots, we can identify the driving factors behind changes in processes, and generalize these changes using compact "style functions". This allows us to understand processes that have limited data at certain time points, by combining the underlying patterns and styles with the appropriate vocabulary, snapshot, and style function. Our evolution analysis method is demonstrated through a case study on process traces related to building a house.

We provide a detailed description of the Kodaira-Parshin compactification for a specific type of mathematical structure called mixed Hodge structures that change with a parameter in an n-dimensional space. This compactification is shown to be closely related to a other type of compact structure developed by Cass, in part by utilizing the concepts from a theorem developed by A. Dimca, O. Randal-Clarke, and the authors. This relationship is expressed through the existence of two continuous mappings in both directions between the Kodaira-Parshin compact structure and the closure of a specific geometric structure within a complex projective space.

A comprehensive NUV-r color-mass diagram has been assembled from approximately 450,000 galaxies using data from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey, covering the period between 2008 and 2018. A distinct upward curvature in the average color of galaxies is observed, particularly above a mass of 10 to the power of 10.6 solar masses, which is attributed to an increasing proportion of spiral and elliptical galaxies in heavier mass clusters. A sharp transition from blue to red in individual galaxy colors is also noted, which corresponds to this mass threshold. Regional variations in the overall galaxy color-mass trend are found, with southern galaxies exhibiting bluer tones than their northern counterparts. Future observations from the James Webb Space Telescope will be instrumental in further investigating these massive galaxies and their evolutionary processes.

A multilingual sentiment analysis (MSA) model that operates across multiple languages and captures underlying opinions is a challenging task. Existing research has concentrated on supervised approaches, where extensive annotated datasets in each target language are necessary. In contrast, this paper presents a pioneering unsupervised sentiment representation learning (USRL) framework, which operates without any sentiment-labeled data in the target language and is fully end-to-end. The proposed framework, called Multilingual Opinion-Sentiment Core Learning (MOSCL), is designed to learn a shared representation that distinguishes between "any non-neutral sentiment" and "neutral" across different source and target languages. The MOSCL framework is evaluated on five English-to-XLSR datasets spanning six different languages and exhibits superior performance compared to current state-of-the-art unsentiment representation learning methods in four out of six target languages. The experimental results highlight the critical role of a shared representation in distinguishing between "any non-neutral sentiment" and "neutral" across different source and target languages.

Identifying high-risk COVID-19 patients who may require ICU admission can significantly enhance the allocation of medical resources. To accomplish this, we developed a machine learning model that predicts ICU admission for COVID-19 patients using data from 14 health indicators. Notably, our model utilizes only longitudinal data up until patient admission, streamlining its applicability in clinical settings. We evaluated two approaches, including a novel method that incorporates dynamic relationships between features. These dynamic models showed superior performance compared to conventional models, with results indicating that rates of feature correlation and decay rates influence the accuracy of predictions. Overall, our study aims to enhance prediction accuracy and provides valuable insights into ICU admission patterns for COVID-19 patients based on their historical health indicator trends.

To establish a connection between the universal bundle functor and the power set monad within the realm of simplicial groups, we have derived this relationship in order to demonstrate that the universal bundle functor indeed forms a strict monad. Furthermore, by examining its structure, we found that its unit and counit endow the category of sets over $X$ as a simplicial group precisely because the universal bundle functor is a monad.

This paper presents new methods for Visual Relationship Detection that address the significant class imbalance in triangular relationship triples. Initially, we introduce a balanced subset of hard triple proposals, which is a crucial step. Next, we develop Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling to handle negative samples for subject and object bounds in bounded relationship triple classification. This is done to mitigate severe optimization difficulties caused by severe imbalance between bound proposals and PPE data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our methods by integrating them into an existing model framework. Through extensive experiments on three standard datasets, MVD, we show that our strategies for balancing proposals significantly enhance performance. Specifically, our improved strategies for bound proposal sampling outperform the baseline FIA model and achieve strong results in visual panorama estimation.

We employ a modified version of the GADGET-3 code, which incorporates a refined two-way coupling between fluid dynamics and stellar particles, to simulate the co-evolution of the Milky Way and a massive galaxy cluster in its group stage. To this end, we create artificial representations of the Milky Way and the cluster galaxy, replicating their observed properties, and integrate them into the cosmological simulation. Our analysis delves into the impact of gas dynamics induced by galaxy movements on the galaxies' structural evolution, particularly focusing on the formation of accretion streams within the surrounding dark matter and gravitational potential wells of the galaxies. Notably, we investigate the profound impact of accretion streams on the galaxies' morphological evolution, demonstrating how stream-induced accretion can give rise to significant star formation, leading to the development of distinct stellar structures such as accretion streams, shells, and giant elliptical galaxies. Furthermore, our research reveals that the galaxies' gravitational potentials evolve as a result of these processes, thereby influencing the galaxies' structural evolution. Our findings carry broad implications for other galaxy-cluster mergers, suggesting that they too can produce significant galaxy structures through similar mechanisms. Ultimately, our study suggests that galaxy-cluster mergers can leave a lasting imprint on galaxies, which can be detected through the observation of massive galaxies residing within galaxy clusters.

This work presents a detailed examination of a significant X16.2 solar flare (A04N07) observed on November 7th, 2004, which was the most powerful solar event in over a decade and a half. The study combines data from multiple sources, including SOHO LASCO, SOHO CDS, SOHO EIT, Yohkoh, RHESSI, GOES, SDO AIA, and STEREO, to provide a comprehensive picture of this event. The X16.2 flare was associated with a powerful M5.4 solar burst and an exceptionally fast coronal mass ejection (CME) with a magnitude of X5.0, resulting in strong G1 solar storms on Earth. The event was characterized by intense emissions across the entire electromagnetic spectrum, from radio waves to gamma rays, and was accompanied by significant radio bursts, including a rare type IV radio burst. The solar activity also triggered significant geomagnetic storms and enhanced radiation levels in space. The data used in this study was obtained from various space missions and ground-based observatories, and the results are presented in various figures and tables. The work is intended to provide a comprehensive understanding of significant solar events and their effects on Earth and space weather.

KIC 9267654, a rapidly rotating K-type star with an equatorial velocity of 100 km/s, presents an atypical rotation pattern where the polar rotation rate is significantly higher than the polar rate seen in other similar stars. The unique structure of this star's atmosphere may be distorted due to its high rotation speed, resulting in a breakdown of traditional cylindrical symmetry and a complex magnetic field configuration. Through the analysis of 11 years of high-precision photometric data from Kepler, the star's complex behavior was uncovered, with two surface patches exhibiting vastly different rotation speeds and characteristics. The extreme tilt of the star's axis of rotation relative to our line of sight allows us to observe the full range of its rotational dynamics. The KIC 9267654 star's behavior could be caused by several factors, including magnetic braking, differential gas flows, and Coriolis effects, making it an ideal subject for further study to understand the physical processes at work in rapidly rotating stars.

The rapid spread of misinformation on social media platforms poses a significant threat to public safety and democratic processes.  With fake news adapting quickly to countermeasures, there is an urgent need for robust, generalizable methods to identify such misinformation.  We propose MetaFEND, a novel framework that leverages Graph Attention Networks to detect fake news across various contexts by learning from auxiliary information, specifically website names associated with news articles.  Our approach utilizes side information networks to capture relationships between attributes and integrates these networks with main networks through cross-network attention mechanisms.  As BERT-based models are commonly used for fake news detection, we also explore a variant of MetaFEND that combines side information networks with BERT, resulting in improved performance.  Our experiments on three datasets demonstrate that MetaFEND outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy.

This study examines a one-dimensional periodic transport equation, free from dissipative effects, and featuring a nonlocal interaction term. We find that this equation produces blow-up phenomena, even at a very basic level. Specifically, for any positive time duration, there exists a smooth, periodic function that satisfies the basic conditions required for solution breakdown. Furthermore, under certain constraints, the solution can reach an infinitely high state in a finite time. These theoretical predictions are also supported by numerical simulations.

This research investigates the problem of finding Golay complementary array pairs (GCAPs) of quaternary type (using symbols 0, 1, -1, and -1) in four dimensions. We establish that GCAPs of quaternary type can only exist for dimensions two and six. By applying the basic idea from the proof, we identify a set of GCAP lengths that satisfy the criteria of being six times a product of primes with remainders of two or three when divided by four. Based on the approach used, we identify methods to construct GCAPs of certain dimensions using matrix transformations, polynomial roots, difference sets, and combinatorial differences.

Utilizing a high-quality and strain-free silicon crystal lattice, the precise positioning of dopants allows for the control of Heisenberg spin exchange interaction. The placement of a magnetic field in an external environment induces a unique relationship between a characteristic spin distance and the field's strength. Exploiting this field-tunable characteristic spin distance enables the formation of a desired, highly connected, and frustrated triangular lattice from a one-dimensional chain of interacting spins. A field-driven, closed quantum system is formed, consisting of an array of highly connected and frustrated spins that can transition between two distinct states representing the presence and absence of a magnetic field, and which can be used to store and process quantum information.

In modern data-rich environments, learning comprehensive models for complex systems has become increasingly feasible, yet applying these systems to new instances remains a challenging task. While traditional methods rely on extrapolating from training data, this paper presents a novel approach to using time series observations as queries in a probabilistic inference framework. By integrating a range of techniques such as Markov logic networks, relational groundings, and relational rules, we demonstrate how to learn and apply a unified framework that can handle both static and dynamic scenarios. Our approach is illustrated through experiments on synthetic data, a gene expression dataset, and a web access pattern dataset, with a focus on evaluating its performance in recovering the underlying structure of new system instances.

A key insight by Quillen and Sullivan established that the cohomology of the topological K-theory group, $BU$, can be viewed as a graded polynomial ring over rational numbers in both integer and smooth homology settings. As a consequence, these settings' structures correspond to collections of partitions distributed across $BU$'s homology. In this paper, we demonstrate that only a finite segment of these homology distributions is necessary to understand the homology of the connective K-theory spectrum, $ku$, within the same settings. Specifically, we show that the homology of $ku$ in both integers and smooth distributions is determined by a finite segment of the $ku$-homology of $BU$ in distributions, which we denote as a finite type setting. Additionally, we establish an isomorphism between the homology of the infinite unitary group, $U$, and the direct sum of a specific distribution setting and the homology of the point, in smooth homology settings. We also extend this result to the $ku$-homology of the unitary group with a finite number of factors, providing a similar isomorphism with the $ku$-homology of the unitary group with a finite number of factors being determined by a finite type setting.

Convolutional neural networks have a strong potential for automatically identifying key areas within medical images, a critical step in various image analysis processes. Although CNN-based methods excel at identifying key elements in images, their performance is significantly limited by the need for extensive training data. Acquiring such data is often impractical in many medical imaging scenarios. To address this challenge, this research explores the use of convolutional neural networks for identifying key areas of interest in medical images with minimal annotated data. The proposed approach combines a feature extraction CNN with a component that models the relationship between images and the key regions they contain. The results show that this method, centered on capturing spatial relationships, yields superior outcomes compared to existing techniques in various low-data medical image segmentation scenarios.

GP 2 is an enhanced version of GP, a high-level language for graph data structures, that features graph mutation operations and supports a wide range of common tasks on complex graphs. GP 2 includes basic building blocks for graph sparsification, a process that transforms dense graphs with repeated elements into leaner, isomorphic sparse graphs that are performance-optimized through a specialized data structure. In this research, we have reworked the specialized data structure, significantly improving its performance while also elevating the performance of several graph mutation operations. Our revised approach involves introducing a new hybrid structure, BigArray, which combines array-like and hash map-like properties and offers a 10-fold performance boost, primarily by eliminating unnecessary array entries. Our performance enhancements are particularly notable for large-scale data sets, where we observed up to a 20-fold improvement, while for smaller data sets, gains of over 1.5-fold were common.

We introduce a new, unified architecture that seamlessly integrates feature extraction methods, whether unsupervised or supervised, through the use of a new loss function. This approach allows for the direct comparison and combination of various feature extraction techniques. Our results demonstrate that our model achieves performance on par with state-of-the-art algorithms when applied to speech, text, and image data. By leveraging our framework's versatility, we make several enhancements to baseline algorithms, including using a modified Attention Is All You Need for text and speech representation, and developing a new co-training method that jointly optimizes a traditional CNN and an attention-based network. This co-training method outperforms our initial starting point by a significant margin.

Inspired by the construction of graph-representations of discrete groups by Woess, we develop methods to create infinite families of graphs with extensive symmetries. Specifically, we define two primary families and ten smaller sub-families of graphs, denoted as $\mathcal{G}$, whose largest symmetries are exhibited as transitive and polynomial growth. Notably, for the majority of these families, we demonstrate that their automorphism groups possess virtually polycyclic structure. Furthermore, we investigate the finite sub symmetries of a compact fixed-point in the maximal symmetries of $\mathcal{G}$, classifying them as either cyclic or paracyclic. Our work builds on previous research, including studies by Downey, Schreiber and Thomas, and Woess.

A data subset can be identified through model selection, which is useful in both
exploratory and controlled studies. Techniques like LARS and logistic regression,
among others, can be enhanced with penalty methods such as Lasso and Group Lasso
to achieve more precise model selection. Our study focuses on the Group Lasso
algorithm, which is applicable to a wide range of data types, both continuous
and categorical. We demonstrate that the algorithm can be employed to select
high-quality models, balancing both model accuracy and simplicity. To do so, we
propose a strategy for determining optimal levels of penalty parameters in both
Gaussian and multinomial logit settings. Simulation studies and real-world data
analysis indicate that models selected using this strategy are both accurate and
high quality.

Recent large language models, equipped with extensive factual knowledge, have achieved significant advancements in various NLP tasks including question answering. Although the emergence of NQA datasets like FAct and ReQA has enabled systematic research on answering non-literal questions, there remains a lack of exploration into diverse data types for pre-training language models. In this study, we investigate the effectiveness of pre-training models using structured data, in our case, a KG, in contrast to common KG-Pre-training methods utilizing text-based entities. In this study, we utilize a KG consisting of non-English statements to ensure robust evaluation of models' linguistic and encoding capabilities. In our experiments, we examine various KG-Pre-training methods and evaluation tasks, employing a range of KGs including both English and non-English statements. Our findings reveal that models with KG-Pre-training excel in KG-based question answering tasks and outperform baselines in KG extension tasks. In contrast, models trained on KGs with non-English statements perform comparably to those trained on text-based data in tasks involving linguistic encoding, in our case, translation. In this study, we contribute several valuable resources for the NQA community, including a comprehensive benchmark dataset and a novel KG-Pre-training framework utilizing statements. This research paper introduces a novel algorithm for rendering lines in a fan shape, which is a challenging task due to the lack of standardization in CSS line rendering specifications. The proposed algorithm employs matrix transformations to effectively display line caps and joins, specifically addressing the rendering of the "arrow" style in combination with other arrow styles such as "first" and "last". To demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm, an example of drawing directed graphs is provided. In contrast to existing solutions that require a nearly linear arrangement of line segments to depict directed graphs, this solution allows for accurate representation of directed graphs while maintaining the "first" and "last" arrow styles.

To effectively enhance speech that is mixed with noise, we introduce a novel Deep Neural Network architecture, the Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network (DPCRN), which leverages the inherent structure of the time-frequency (TF) domain and efficiently models both short-term and long-term non-stationary speech characteristics.  By integrating Dual-Path Convolution (DPC) blocks, our network captures the local non-stationary patterns within the TF structure using separate short-term and long-term pathways, each with distinct filter settings.  Furthermore, we incorporate a Dual-Path Convolution Cyclic Permutation (DPC-CP) mechanism to further unravel the inherent structure of the TF representation. To model short-term sequential dependencies, we introduce Dual-Path Convolution Long Short-Term Memory (DPC-LSTM) modules into the short-term pathway. Due to the efficient design of DPC blocks, the DPCRN architecture can directly utilize the TF representation of the noisy speech, avoiding the need for a Time-to-Frequency (T2F) transformation and Time-to-Time (T2T) transformation, and resulting in reduced computational cost. The two-fluid model is a simple approach to describe the two-scale behavior of
turbulent fluids. In the context of Rayleigh-Bénard convection, our analysis of
this model reveals its limitations and intriguing connections to other theories.
However, the model fails to replicate the correct $2/7$ power law for Naviar-Stokes number scaling of the
nutational shell's heat flux, as it predicts a $1$ scaling. The model also reveals
interesting connections to existing theories, including the connection between the
two-shell model and the double diffusion model, as well as the relationship
between the one-fluid model and the single diffusion model. The two-fluid model's
assumptions can be relaxed, as seen in the double diffusion model, which allows
for the thermal shell to exhibit temporal and spatial variability. The model's
breakdown at high Rayleigh numbers can be attributed to the violation of its
underlying assumptions, as seen in the case of the one-scale turbulent fluid.

A two-step quantum protocol is outlined for creating a specific type of entangled state between a cavity and several atoms that interact with the cavity from a distance. Initially, the cavity swaps its entanglement with an atom entering the cavity, and in the second step, the cavity swaps its interaction with a distant atom. By leveraging two distant interactions that do not correlate with each other, we can turn its weak coupling with the atoms into a potential for creating a specific multipartent entanglement state. Even when the interactions are not correlated, we find that a certain level of entanglement exists among the atoms. If the interactions are switched on in a particular pattern, we can completely remove a specific type of unwanted entanglement, and also improve the previously achieved entanglement. If the interactions are completely uncorrelated, we can improve the previously achieved entanglement by around thirty percent.

Social media platforms, like Twitter, enable individuals to freely express their opinions, making sentiment analysis in this environment a valuable tool for monitoring public opinion and tracking events. Although several studies have attempted to develop methods for analyzing the sentiment of tweets, the lack of high-quality datasets with accurate annotations remains a significant obstacle. This study aims to create a new, comprehensive dataset containing 100,000 manually labeled tweets, categorized into five sentiment classes: positive, negative, neutral, humorous, and controversial. To ensure the dataset's diversity and representativeness, we employed a combination of manual and automated annotation techniques, using existing datasets to guide the process. The result is a novel, representative dataset for sentiment analysis research, which was evaluated through a comparative study of various LSTM models, demonstrating the new dataset's utility for analyzing sentiment in social media content.

A new non-linear Yang-Mills charge parameter is explored in the context of four-dimensional Reissner-Nordstr\"om anti-de Sitter (AdS) black holes, which are characterized by both their mass and Yang-Mills charge. Calculating the non-linear Yang-Mills charge's impact on both shadow appearance and Hawking radiation (thermal profile) of these black holes in anti-de Sitter space, researchers found that radiation properties are more significantly affected than the visual appearance of the black hole shadow. This effect varies depending on the specific radii of the surrounding space in which the black holes exist.

A new method is proposed to identify and quantify nonclassical characteristics of both quantum and classical composite systems using optical tomographic techniques. This approach leverages a measure of entanglement that accounts for nonclassical characteristics, even in the absence of quantum correlations. By applying this technique to a system composed of two independent thermal sources, a significant manifestation of nonclassical effects is observed, where the system becomes entangled when a specific threshold of nonclassicality is reached. This development could have a transformative impact on quantum technology applications, such as quantum communication and metrology.

Viewers of immersive videos often struggle to pinpoint their focus due to the vast field of view that video players offer. This difficulty is especially pronounced when viewers attempt to locate specific objects within the video stream. As a result, viewport prediction is essential for developing efficient streaming solutions that prioritize areas of interest and minimize bandwidth consumption when unneeded parts go out of view. This study investigates how video subtitles impact viewport patterns and prediction accuracy. Subtitle impact is examined in two distinct scenarios: synchronized and unsynchronized subtitles. Experiments involving 2433 video clips from the YouTube dataset, with 9609 viewports tracked through eye-tracking technology, reveal that the presence of subtitles can both enhance and hinder viewport prediction accuracy. Furthermore, viewer behavior analysis uncovers that some viewers tend to fixate on subtitle text, whereas others navigate the video without being influenced by their presence. This behavior is further explored in relation to viewer expertise and the size of their viewports.

We have developed a set of techniques to produce thermal equilibrium states and time-evolved systems through partial peptide optimization (PEPO). This is achieved directly in a vector representing the thermal state, with no need for additional steps. The method involves constructing structured tensor networks known as peptide posets (PEPOs). These PEPOs have a significantly smaller bond dimension than traditional methods, particularly when dealing with large systems that have periodic boundaries in both space and time. Compared to standard thermal states and evolved systems, these PEPOs are more efficient in terms of computational resources. Additionally, we have established ways to convert thermal PEPOs into accurate representations of equilibrium states within the same computational framework. This conversion process is more computationally affordable than converting evolved PEPOs. When applied to the thermal PEPOs, we have found that the resulting states can accurately represent systems at high temperatures and with Periodic Boundary Conditions (PBC). These features make thermal PEPOs an attractive area of research.

We provide a new method for constructing canonical surfaces in the decoupling context, leveraging Taylor-based analysis to investigate the impact of varying order polynomials. By sufficiently narrowing the decoupling scale for low-order polynomials and justifying broader decoupling for higher orders, our approach asystetically extends Bourgain-Demeter's results for $p < 6$. Additionally, it continues the DEC method for larger values of $p$. A key component of our approach involves developing a local decoupling estimate with precise details, which draws on Keel-Tao's bound for the singular integral operator associated with the Airy equation to achieve optimal decay for an artificial term derived from a function's expansion.

A significant issue with the operator product expansion (OPE) is that it cannot be applied to deep inelastic scattering (DIS) at high energies due to the one-to-one correspondence between perturbative coefficients and non-perturbative effects being broken by a cluster of poles in the infrared renormalons.  To address this problem, we propose that a corresponding operator must be added to the original set of twist-2 operators, specifically introducing an infinite tower of higher-twist operators, including one with defined positivity properties and an associated forward matrix element that resembles a gluon distribution, exhibiting a characteristic power-suppression behavior.  Notably, this particular operator may play a crucial role in the Gerasimov-Drell-Hearn (GDH) sum rule, which has an unusually large residual term and a slowly converging expansion in terms of twist, as this operator could potentially account for both features.

We investigated how a single layer of magnetized grating modifies light propagation in a magnetophotonic crystal structure. Our research focused on the strong interaction between the surface waves and the Rayleigh anomaly within the periodic pattern, which results in a complex exchange between reflected and transmitted light. We observed that this interaction creates a mixed anomaly that retains its sensitivity to magnetic fields in both reflected and transmitted light, providing a robust basis for developing magnetic field sensors with enhanced accuracy.

This research introduces a novel approach, termed Decision-based Black-box Knowledge Distillation (DB3), to enhance the accuracy of low-capacity decision engines without requiring access to their training data or matching architectures with more capable models. In the case of black-box systems, a high-capacity model is trained using only input outputs from the target, leveraging a unique method that relaxes the requirement of matching input patterns. Through simulation, the proposed DB3 approach demonstrates superior performance compared to conventional counterfactual explanation techniques and traditional knowledge distillation methods.

Researchers examined selected $B^0_s$ meson decays into either $K^0_S$ and $\pi^0$ or $K_0^*$ and $\pi^0$, specifically focusing on $B^0_s \rightarrow K^0_S \pi^0$, $B^0_s \rightarrow K_0^{*}(892)^0 \pi^0$, and various other similar decay modes. Additionally, $B^0$ meson decays into the same final states were studied. Using data collected at specific collision energies, they observed several decay modes and gathered information on others. The uncertainty in these measurements is primarily due to the amount of data available for study.

Let $H$ be a group that is finite and let $W$ be a multiplicity free module belonging to $H$. Suppose $H$ is a subgroup of a larger group $G$ and $M$ is a composition factor of $W$ when viewed as being under $G$. We can relate the "depth" of a particular submodule of $W$ that is isomorphic to $M$ with respect to $H$ to the "depth" of the same submodule with respect to $G$ by a specific formula. Also, we can reconstruct a part of the submodule structure of $W$ when viewed under $G$ based on the H-H submodule structure of $W$ and certain other information related to $H$ and $G$.

Mimicry while performing complex tasks can effectively be accomplished, but complex tasks often require extensive data for training and safety can't always be guaranteed. Co-iteration learning enables an agent to master a diverse range of skills through collaboration with another agent, even in real-world settings. We introduce Co-Imitation Learning, a method that combines the agent's observations with those of another agent using a neural network, and optimizes this approach by trying out different combinations of the two data sources. Our Co-Imitation Learning approach outperforms traditional methods on multiple Co-itation benchmarks, including those featuring partially observable Markov decision processes, and demonstrates improved safety and sample efficiency.

We investigate the performance of the Altes and Woster sequential decoding algorithm, which we modify to accommodate a varying cutoff rate during decoding. We observe that this method's outcome heavily relies on the chosen rate, which we define as a parameter in order to analyze its effects. We also demonstrate how a rate set to the rate polarized to its probability of making an error provides a optimized setting that, in turn, guarantees improved performance.

Reinforcement learning (TR) has been applied to various non-Markovian sequence tasks, including machine translation, where the reward is determined by a reference translation. In this approach, a policy gradient method is used, initially guided by a right-to-left reward function trained with an actor-critic model. Subsequently, the action space is optimized through a postprocessing step. While this three-step strategy has been shown to improve translation quality, the role of the action space optimization step remains unclear. To better understand this, we conducted a simplified reward model using a right-to-left reward, actor-critic, and action space optimization steps, applied to the baseline data without any further processing. Our findings from this study reveal that the action space optimization step is not universally beneficial, and in fact, performing a postprocessing step can sometimes degrade performance. We also explored several potential explanations for this behavior and proposed a more effective two-step strategy that reinforces TR by eliminating the action space optimization step. We discovered that removing this step can significantly enhance performance across multiple translation tasks.

A quantum analog of a thermostatic system environment-which regulates
the flow of information in both directions between an external quantum system
and its surroundings-is described and analyzed in this work. A quantum feedback
loop, which facilitates the two-way exchange of information between the system
and its surroundings, acts as this surrounding. The relationship between the
regulatory capabilities of the loop and its constituent parts-the external
system's degree of randomness and the loop's delay time-is established in this
work. Furthermore, a specific quantum loop based on a pair of mutually
interacting m-mode Gaussian fields, which exhibit delayed self-interaction, is
proposed to demonstrate that a two-way exchange of a specific quantity of field
quadratures is directly proportional to the time delay when viewed in its
steady state. Because of its direct proportionality to the time delay, this
quantum loop, which is characterized by its linearity, is particularly useful
for applications that require a exchange of information in both directions.

We investigate biharmonic hypersurfaces within Euclidean space that satisfy a specific curvature criterion, where the Laplacian operator appears in a biharmonic equation, influenced by the choice of Laplacian definition. When a recurrent operator is absent, all such hypersurfaces are minimal, thus demonstrating the operator's impact on minimizing these biharmonic properties.

This research focuses on identifying which subsets of Euclidean space can be defined using a specific type of automated system, known as p/q-recognisers. These systems can correctly identify subsets of points in d-dimensional space with rational coordinates, based on a modular rule that varies depending on the denominator. A significant finding from our work is a generalisation of a previous result, demonstrating that p/q-recognisable subsets can be described as unions of linear subspaces. This generalisation holds true for subsets of Euclidean space and also extends to subsets of broader algebraic structures, including modules over rings. A key tool in our approach is a lemma that explores the properties of a specific mathematical construct called the P_P/q, which consists of elements that are uniquely identifiable due to their distinct P-adic representations. This construct is shown to be isomorphic to another mathematical construct, U, with unique rational representations, and a tool called Berstel's theorem is used to solve a specific problem involving p/q-recognisable problems.

The primary goal of this research paper is to clarify how the WIREDTIGER, REPLICASET, and SHARDEDCLUSTER MongoDB configurations comply with various snapshot isolation concurrency control methods. To achieve this, we collected information from the official MongoDB documentation and research articles, then created formal models for each configuration's data structure and replication behavior. Next, we used these models to verify the consistency of our findings with the documented specifications. Additionally, we demonstrated how our models can be applied to software tool outputs, such as those from the DBTest testing tool, to validate the accuracy of our assumptions.

For any two-coloring of a complete graph, the chromatic symmetric function captures the symmetry and structure of colorings with respect to different colors. A specific study shows that when this function is expressed in a modified basis, its coefficients match a specific combinatorial quantity made up of steps in certain path patterns. This match is found after applying a mathematical operation known as the Hilbert series, which is used to describe the structure of a ring generated by monomial symmetric functions. This finding extends an earlier discovery made by Gaubert and Sheth.

The main findings of an experiment involving Ising spins arranged in a hexagonal lattice with elastic connections are displayed. The hysteresis loop observed in this study exhibits a complex structure, the components of which can be explained by the cooperative behavior of the spins within the triangular networks of the hysteresis loop. Furthermore, this study utilizes a Monte Carlo simulation to characterize the hysteresis loop's intricate features, revealing that the loop's structure serves as a valuable indicator of spin network dynamics, ultimately demonstrating that the spin network behaves like an external, observable property.

A study on interplanetary proton populations characterizes their energy distributions at two locations, near 1 AU and very close to the Sun. A Monte Carlo model was used to evaluate energy necessary for protons to escape solar gravity at both locations. Near 1 AU, distinct distributions were observed for protons trapped in the solar wind, those forming the background, and those responsible for geomagnetic storms, all following a non-degenerative Maxwellian pattern. A heliocentric study found energy required to escape solar gravity follows a pattern similar to the wind's own distribution, with a notable difference between trapped protons and those background in the solar wind. A robust link exists between the distribution of escape-necessary energy and solar wind distribution. A study of solar flutes found that S-shaped features in spectral lines are caused by protemperatures, with a small to large heliocentric distance. S-shaped features are more pronounced in Fe X than in Fe XIII.

Neural Emotion Adapters (NEA) is a pre-trained model that excels in low-resource multilingual emotion recognition tasks. It allows for efficient adaptation to various languages and data sets without modifying its core components. In our enhanced version, we incorporate additional modules that enhance the model's adaptability to different languages and datasets. In contrast to the original method, which uses a separate module for each language, our approach employs a lightweight attention mechanism. This mechanism enables a subset of NEA's parameters to be repurposed for recognition tasks across multiple languages. Additionally, we include a set of external parameters to further enhance the model's adaptability. Experimental results on four English and six non-English datasets demonstrate that our enhanced model consistently achieves superior performance.

The adiabatic evolution of a strong shock wave in an environment with changing conditions is studied, particularly when the environment changes suddenly. When a strong shock wave propagates through a space that is expanding or contracting, it experiences sudden transitions, including possible instabilities, which are analyzed mathematically. By examining exact solutions to the shock wave equations, we find that, similar to an adiabatic homogenous system, it can exhibit both expansions and contractions, which can also be further complicated by phase transitions at the boundaries. These boundary conditions are influenced by the characteristics of the surrounding environment.

Researchers have developed a method to create a class of one-dimensional supersymmetric quantum potentials without singularities, based on the harmonic oscillator and classified using the polynomial Heisenberg algebra. This study defines these potentials using shape invariance and verifies their properties, such as exact solutions to Schrödinger equations and essential spectral characteristics. It has been proven that these potentials can be described using the polynomial Heisenberg algebra and their SUSY partners, which can be generated through the algebra with specific choice of parameters. This class of potentials includes various known potentials, and their SUSY counterparts, with exact solutions and additional characteristics. They can be further generalized using the $q$-deformed Heisenberg algebra. This research has significant implications for understanding the Hosokawa and Kawakami potentials, which were previously derived using the shape invariance method. It has been found that these potentials, along with their SUSY partners, can be obtained using the polynomial Heisenberg algebra with specific parameters. This work also explores their properties, such as exact Schrödinger equations solutions, the harmonic oscillator as a limiting case, and their behavior at large distances. This research has far-reaching applications in physics, including astrophysics, where it has been applied to model the large radius behavior of neutron stars.

In this work, we develop a method to Lyapunov exponents in a way that aligns with measure-theoretic concepts, enabling the study of pointwise Lyapunov exponents and the stability of orbital dynamics within complex systems. Our innovative approach allows us to calculate the leading Lyapunov exponent of any given trajectory by directly integrating a raywise Lyapunov function, a forward-looking trajectory simulation solution. This approach bypasses the traditional requirement of possessing an explicit analytical representation of the underlying dynamical system, thereby accommodating a wide range of problems from simple orbital dynamics to highly intricate applications such as black hole chaos and curved space simulations.

In the context of non-abelian aether theory, also known as the Gribov-Nielsen aether, we modify the standard non-abelian aether term by adding a second term, the square of the curl of the gauge field. By examining the theory in a one-loop correction to QCD within a one-loop effective action framework, we find that it leads to substantial changes in the non-abelian version of the Stefan-Boltzmann law and the Casimir energy. Moreover, we explore how varying the dimensionality of spacetime impacts these results.

An example using the Heston model demonstrates the calculation of the before-hedging expected cost for a European option and a portfolio.

The recent advancements in flat cable technology and power converters enable the beam-beam closed orbit to be made precise to within 100 microns over the entire interaction region. This level of accuracy is crucial for achieving the nominal beam-beam optics and for detecting any unexpected beam-beam effects. As a starting point, this paper outlines the measurable impacts of beam-beam interactions, including intrinsic mode coupling, tune shift, and beam breakup. It also highlights the critical need for precise beam-beam closed orbit to exploit these discoveries. A review of existing methods and their limitations for measuring beam-beam closed orbit is presented, paving the way for a proposed solution. This solution presents the principle, design, and expected performance of a new device called beam position monitor with integrated beam-beam effect, which is capable of directly and precisely measuring beam-beam closed orbit. It is demonstrated that this new device can meet the required beam-beam closed orbit precision at the PEP-X.

This research develops a robust algorithm for distributed optimization, designed to handle communication interference from malicious agents. It focuses on a setting where most agents are honest, equipped with secure communication channels, but some agents are compromised and can manipulate the messages between honest agents. Despite these manipulations, the honest agents maintain communication with each other through a time-varying network. We develop an algorithm that allows the honest agents to reach a consensus on a minimizer of a combined objective function, using only local information. It does this without needing to know about the specific communication network structure, the number of agents, or the specifics of the interference being caused. We demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness in a simulated scenario, where agents with varying objective functions are located in different areas and need to find a common solution.

The upcoming generation of large-scale surveys like Euclid, DESI, and the Vera Rubin Observatory will produce massive datasets that are both complex and abundant. As these projects generate enormous amounts of information, it becomes crucial to anticipate and manage potential instrumental biases before data collection begins. This paper explores the potential for leveraging machine learning techniques to simulate instrumental effects more realistically, focusing on two key areas: creating realistic input images and developing models to represent their impacts. By incorporating these effects into training datasets, researchers can improve the accuracy of cosmological inferences drawn from future surveys. This approach has already shown promise in addressing image reconstruction challenges and can also be applied to other phenomena such as point spread functions and spectral distortions. Although not yet fully implemented, these techniques can be tested on existing surveys and have the potential to significantly enhance the accuracy of upcoming cosmological research.

The BART architecture, which is a sequential model, has shown superior performance in predicting partial tree structures compared to traditional parsing approaches that also rely on constituency parses. However, its effectiveness in predicting word order alone, a simpler task from constitutive parses, contradicts findings that sequential models struggle with partial tree structures. This discrepancy prompts an examination of the connections between these two tasks and an assessment of BART's performance using a detailed dataset.

Our new approach, called Multi-Domain Deepfake Detection Network with Cross-Stitch Connections (MDDC), is designed to effectively combat emerging deepfake types by adapting to novel data distributions. To adapt to different data types, our network incorporates dynamic cross-stitch connections that merge existing knowledge with new information. Specifically, we develop a projection mechanism to align existing and new feature spaces, and a learning mechanism to integrate aligned features. Our proposed method yields substantial performance boosts of 6.4 and 8.15 GB when tested on two challenging scenarios. Moreover, our framework offers an interpretable understanding of how the network adapts to new data by visualizing the learned features and learning parameters.

Additionally, it helped establish that the class of tori,, possessing spaces from $\mathcal{P}$,, could be conformally embedded in a higher-dimensional Euclidean space,.

These results generalize earlier findings by Cohen and the author, and a key component of our proof involves applying Chebotarev's density theorem to solve systems of equations.

Forsage, a high-returns online program, is indicative of the digital transformation of complex financial pyramidal schemes. Despite its apparent profitability, the scheme's structure inevitably results in substantial losses for the majority of its participants, according to an analysis of its documentation and online discourse. Data from Reddit and Twitter were gathered and analyzed to examine the discussion surrounding Forsage, with results revealing that more than 90% of users end up experiencing losses, while a minority of highly rewarded "top earners" receive significant financial gains. These findings are further complicated by observations of misinformation, forum manipulation, and denial of the pyramidal nature of the scheme. Given their vulnerability to deception and financial harm, it is crucial to better understand and address the root causes behind such misinformation and delusion.

This study investigates 11 potential globular clusters in the Milky Way, including NGC 6092, NGC 6204, and NGC 6218, among others. We used four different methods to determine the ages of these clusters, finding that results from multiple techniques generally agree. However, some clusters, like NGC 6204 and NGC 6218, have ages that diverge significantly, by a factor of ten, when assessed using different methods. We found that the age of these clusters can vary widely, spanning ten orders of magnitude, and caution is advised in interpreting them as genuine globular clusters without further investigation. Nevertheless, for clusters with consistent ages across different methods, we can draw more reliable conclusions. For instance, NGC 6092 and NGC 6264 have ages estimated at around 9 billion years, whereas NGC 6204 is younger, at approximately 400 million years. We also discovered that the colour of these clusters can differ substantially, with colours ranging from 0.4 to 2.5 in the $(u-g)_0$ colour, and that their radii are comparable to those of well-known clusters, with an average value of approximately 12 solar radii.

If $O$ is a set of transformations that form either a group or semigroup, and T is a tensor acting as an error correction code within $O$, we investigate tensor networks composed of multiple instances of $O$-valued actions, including $T$, to better understand composite quantum error correction codes made of multiple quantum Ising machines. In particular, if the network contains only one type of action that forms a semigroup and serves as a perfect quantum Ising machine, we prove it must be equivalent to a single instance of that action, provided the network's dimensions are not excessively large. In addition, if the network includes two actions that together can reconstruct any target state and has a size within its capacity to correct errors, we can simplify the network to a single instance of a combined action that can also act as a perfect quantum Ising machine. These findings are applicable to physical systems like the photonic T-state.

Predicting future process instances is crucial for process management, yet existing methods generally produce one-size-fits-all outcomes, ignoring the varied outcomes that result from different starting points.  To address this issue, we developed a novel approach called Conditional Process Outcome Prediction (CPREP), which uses conditional deep neural networks to create a framework for generating multiple process outcome predictions from a single process instance.  Our results, based on three process mining datasets, demonstrate that performance of prediction models can differ significantly across process process segments, and that our method provides valuable, diverse predictions that can support process management decision-making.

This research focuses on estimating the Fourier transforms of functions with rate-limiting growth in both time and frequency domains, characterized by Gelfand-Shilov spaces. We establish growth limitations for the Fourier transforms of these functions, which also belong to a related class with slightly less restrictive constraints. Notable applications include examining the time-domain behavior of solutions to the damped wave equation and discrete Schrödinger operators.

We investigated the intensity and width of a star's hydrogen emission line to understand what occurs during a stellar flare, specifically for GJ 382. We analyzed 9.5 hours of data, examining the relationship between the emission line's width and its surrounding space's temperature, as well as the line's broadening and the star's spin. Flares caused significant increases in line width, with some peaks matching the star's estimated rotational velocity. However, we found that line width variations did not correlate with ultraviolet radiation, indicating that other mechanisms, such as impact or shear, must be responsible for observed line broadening. Additionally, we found that emission line profiles did not match expectations based on the star's spin, suggesting that other factors, such as stellar spots, influenced our measurements. Flares also caused increases in line width that did not diminish over time, with some lasting for hours. We found that a significant portion of stars in the local neighborhood, including nearby stars, may exhibit similar behaviors, and further research is needed to determine their effects on planetary atmospheres.

Deep point cloud models are vulnerable to label-misclassification due to malicious label-twisting schemes. A malicious adversary can force a victim to classify a data point as belonging to any set of target classes by supplying a set of corresponding lure statements. While previous defensive strategies have been developed to counter this threat, they are all assessed under a single evaluation metric and a singular framework. In contrast, this paper introduces a comprehensive evaluation framework called TPRS to evaluate the robustness of a defensive strategy against any form of plausible label-space manipulation by a malicious adversary. Furthermore, this study explores the feasibility of using a simple linear separator to counter label-twisting attacks and finds that this approach results in a significantly lower certified resistance to such attacks compared to the original evaluation framework. All these findings are validated using extensive experiments conducted on widely used datasets including ModelNet10 and ShapeNet.

model and a known non-linear relationship. This linear model with controls can 
serve as a substitute for the Koopman operator model. We introduce data-driven 
control synthesis approaches that are grounded in the knowledge that our linear

through numerical examples.

Neural text generation models often produce average sentences by implicitly combining multiple interpretations into single probability distributions, making it difficult to effectively leverage prior language knowledge for enhancement. Drawing a comparison to GANs, our proposed SparseGAN model aims to represent the diversity of possible sentences under a non-unique mapping from sentences to distributions. In this framework, some sentences are connected to specific probability distributions, while others remain unaccounted for. To illustrate, consider the task of news headline generation from articles: heads that share core content form a dense cluster, but heads covering distinct stories constitute scattered points. As a result, the distribution forms sparse GAN-like structure. To implement this model, we develop a two-stage training process. In the first stage, a strong text generator is trained using standard techniques. In the second stage, a diversity discriminator is trained to distinguish heads that the generator has already produced from new ones, and a reinforcement learning generator is then added to generate heads that pass the discriminator's test. Experimental results on Chinese corpus show that Text generation benefits significantly from this approach, producing more diverse and coherent outputs.

The concept of interstellar panspermia, where microorganisms are dispersed between galaxies, is influenced by various stellar environments. However, short-lived, unstable stellar environments like novae, supernovae, and gamma-ray bursts are unlikely to support such dispersal due to their explosive nature. A detailed examination of various stellar events reveals that many outcomes, including those of nova explosions, supernovae, gamma-ray bursts, tidal disruption events, and even some stellar flares, are likely to create lethal environments that could destroy any microorganisms. Conversely, events like Type Ia supernovae, Type II supernovae, and long gamma-ray bursts are found to have low probabilities of allowing for the survival of microorganisms within a safe distance range. Nevertheless, certain types of novae, specifically Iax and IX events, along with some gamma-ray bursts and tidal disruption events, are identified as more favorable stellar environments that could contribute to the dispersal of interstellar life. These events, occurring with a frequency of 0.01 to 1 per millennium within a galaxy, are more likely to support the survival of microorganisms within a safe distance range of 1 to 10 parsecs, making them the most favorable stellar environments for evaluating the feasibility of interstellar life dispersal.

A novel R-based package, named 'rSCR', has been developed to create spatial capture-recapture models within the R statistical computing environment. This package utilizes an object-oriented structure and can handle various data types through custom methods. It includes an advanced density estimation technique based on active detection, which builds on existing software but offers enhanced functionality. The package also features a basic density estimation method similar to an R equivalent of another program, with improved data handling capabilities. Developers can easily extend the package's functionality due to its well-documented source code structure. The authors demonstrate the package's utility by analyzing an dataset containing radio-collar data from red foxes, with all code publicly available for replication purposes.

A key challenge in multilayer network models with node states governed by coupled dynamics across network layers is assessing state stability. To address this, a streamlined method is proposed for evaluating stability by breaking down the Jacobian matrix into a core coupled component and a diagonal matrix representing individual network components, thus facilitating stability assessment through the proposed network's effective coupling strength threshold. This threshold, when met, ensures network state replicability, a property that can be beneficial in various applications, including training artificial brain networks. A neural network model trained across multiple independent networks with initially random, potentially inconsistent states demonstrates state synchronizability, a desirable feature for transferring learned knowledge between networks while preserving consistency.

Given two differential module categories, denoted as $\mathsf{Mod}_{K[\partial]}$ and $\mathsf{Mod}_{L[\partial']}$ where $K$ and $L$ are fields, and a differential operator $d = \frac{\partial}{\partial t} + P(\partial)$ with coefficients in $K$, we define a functor $\Phi$ that maps left $K[\partial, \frac{\partial}{\partial t}]$-differential modules to left $L[\partial']$-differential modules. Building on the work of D'Alessio, who linked the kernel of $\Phi$ to the division property of the operator $d$ when $K=L$, we investigate multiple scenarios and define an operator $d'$ with coefficients in $L$ such that $\Phi$ can be characterized by keeping the subcategory of $\mathsf{Mod}_{L[\partial,\frac{\partial}{\partial t}]}$ where the operator $\frac{\partial}{\partial t}$ is invertible. If $\Phi$ is a perfect relative to the functor defined by $d'$, then the operator $d'$ is considered parametrized by $d$.

This study introduces ARTIS, a new platform for developing and assessing code
location error-finding systems. The ARTIS environment simulates a realistic
scenario where programmers are required to identify incorrect code snippets that
have been inserted into a correct base, which in turn contains various
distractor code segments that have been incorrectly inserted. The automated
tooling developed for this purpose aids in locating and correcting these errors.
The code location error-finding system we created leverages this platform, which
is designed to be easily adaptable. The testing environment allows us to identify
and correct mistakes, as well as incrementally improve our algorithm. The
testing framework is also straightforward to customize, which allows us to
manually correct code and incrementally correct code locations errors, as well as
examine how the system performs on different levels of difficulty. The difficulty
is determined by the percentage of the correct code, which in turn is influenced
by the size of the code snippets that have been incorrectly inserted. The
comprehensive testing framework in the ARTIS platform allows us to efficiently
generate a large number of code instances that have been incorrectly inserted,
which in turn enables us to evaluate our code location error-finding system on
thousands of code instances. The system we created and the associated
documentation for the ARTIS platform are available on GitHub.

In the Lie algebras or groups of types $A_l$ and $D_l$, there is a particularly large root, the maximal root, which commutes with all other roots in the system. We demonstrate that, for both Lie algebras and groups of types $A_l$ and $D_l$, the maximal algebra generated by the maximal root alone is isomorphic to the algebra with a single isomorphism. Moreover, we can generalize this isomorphism for the "almost maximal" roots in types $A_l$ and $D_l$.
